generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Launched in 1953 with a six-cylinder and a two-speed automatic, the sports car part came later. The 1957 fuel-injected 283 made one horsepower per cubic inch, the number that made Corvette credible.

generations.name: Second generation (Sting Ray)
generations.note: The Sting Ray: a knife-edge coupe with hidden headlights and, for 1963 only, the split rear window. Independent rear suspension, disc brakes from 1965, and the 427 big-block turned it into a genuine world-beater.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: The longest-lived Corvette, wearing Mako Shark show-car curves over C2 bones. Early chrome-bumper cars are the athletes; the seventies brought emissions-era power cuts, and the shape carried the car through regardless.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: A clean-sheet, aerodynamics-first redesign that made handling the headline. The 1990 ZR-1 answered with a Lotus-designed, quad-cam LT5 built by Mercury Marine, 405 hp by the end of the run and a 24-hour endurance record to prove it.

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: Hydroformed frame rails, a rear transaxle, and the new LS V8: stiffer, lighter, faster. The Z06 of 2001 revived the badge as a fixed-roof track car with 405 hp in final form.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Exposed headlights for the first time since 1962, and performance that kept climbing: the 7.0-litre Z06 at 505 hp, then the supercharged ZR1 at 638 hp, the fastest production Corvette of the front-engine era.

generations.name: Seventh generation
generations.note: The last front-engine Corvette, and a high point: the Stingray's 455 hp LT1, then the 650 hp supercharged Z06. Manual take rate stayed high because the buyers demanded it.

generations.name: Eighth generation
generations.note: Mid-engine at last, after decades of prototypes. The flat-plane-crank Z06's 5.5L V8 revs to 8,600 rpm and makes 670 hp without turbos or supercharging.

models.intro: America's attainable supercar since 1953. The Corvette's trick has always been the arithmetic: most of a European exotic's speed for a fraction of the price. The C8's move to a mid-engine layout in 2020 broke a 67-year tradition and nobody sensible misses the old one.

models.collectorNote: First-generation cars are the blue-chip end; a documented Z/28 or big-block SS is the one to own. Of the modern cars, the sixth-gen ZL1 1LE is the future collectible, low production, extreme aero, manual available.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: The 1969 model is the high-water mark, hidden headlights on the RS, the DZ 302 in the Z/28, and big-block SS cars that are still the reference for what a pony car should look like.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: Aero-slick and underrated for years. The 1998 LS1 cars took the engine that redefined the segment, and the SS and WS6-adjacent specials are finally getting their due.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: On the Alpha platform shared with Cadillac's sports sedans, and it showed, this is the best-handling Camaro ever built. The ZL1's 650 hp supercharged LT4 made it a supercar argument with a bowtie on it.

models.intro: GM's answer to the Mustang, launched for 1967 and locked in the pony-car war for six generations. Production ended again in 2024 with no successor announced, the sixth generation went out as the best-driving Camaro ever made.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: The Silverado name became the standalone truck line in 1999, replacing the C/K. The LS-family small-blocks in these trucks are a big part of why that engine family is everywhere now.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: Direct injection, cylinder deactivation, and a properly modern cabin. The 6.2L versions were quietly among the quickest stock trucks of their era.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: A turbo four-cylinder as the volume engine, unthinkable in a full-size truck a generation ago, with the 6.2L V8 and the 3.0L Duramax diesel at the top of the range.

models.intro: Chevrolet's full-size truck and Ford's oldest argument. Chevrolet pickups go back to 1918, but the Silverado nameplate dates to 1999, when it replaced the C/K line. The 3.0L Duramax diesel is the connoisseur's pick; the 6.2L V8 is the loud one.

models.collectorNote: The '57 is the icon and priced like it, fuel-injected cars and convertibles sit at the top. A '55 or '56 hardtop gives you the same Tri-Five experience for noticeably less money.

generations.name: Tri-Five (second generation)
generations.note: 1955, '56, '57, the cars that defined the era. The 1957 model's fins, gold anodised grille, and available fuel injection made it the most reproduced piece of 1950s Americana there is.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: The jet-age Bel Air: quad headlights, big fins in 1959 with those famous teardrop taillights, and the Impala name splitting off above it as the range-topper.

models.intro: Chevrolet's top trim line through the 1950s, and the 1955–1957 'Tri-Five' cars are about as close as American design gets to universal agreement. The '57 Bel Air is shorthand for the whole decade.

models.collectorNote: Two separate collector stories: the 1960s SS big-block cars, and the 1994–1996 Impala SS, a blacked-out, LT1-powered B-body that has been climbing steadily for a decade. The front-drive cars after 2000 are used cars, not collectibles.

generations.name: Second generation (SS era)
generations.note: The Super Sport arrived in 1961 and the big-block cars defined American full-size performance: the 409 first, then the 396 and 427. A 1964 SS hardtop is the one in every song for a reason.

generations.name: Seventh generation (Impala SS)
generations.note: One model, three years, essentially one spec: the Caprice-based, LT1-powered Impala SS of 1994–1996. 260 hp, floor shifter from 1996, and a cult following that never faded.

generations.name: Tenth generation
generations.note: The last Impala: a genuinely good full-size sedan, especially with the 305 hp 3.6L V6, killed by the crossover market along with every other big sedan GM made.

models.intro: Chevrolet's flagship nameplate from 1958, and the best-selling car in America through the mid-1960s, over a million sold in 1965 alone. It lived three lives: the 1960s icon, the 1990s Impala SS sleeper, and a competent front-drive sedan until 2020.
